pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey on the Solway in Cumberland, founded 1150 as a daughter of Melrose; its nave survives as the parish church of Abbeytown)
etymology: Old Norse holmr, an island or water-meadow, with a Cumbric element; the water-meadow of Cultram, on the marshy Solway plain.
biblical_def: Holm Cultram was founded in 1150 on the Solway marshes of Cumberland, a daughter of the Scottish house of Melrose and so a border abbey in every sense — raided by Scots armies, holding lands on both sides, and keeping the body of Robert the Bruce's father in its church. At the dissolution the local people petitioned to keep the nave, because it was their parish church and their shelter against raiders, and they kept it: it is the parish church of Abbeytown to this day, having survived a roof fire as recently as 2006. That continuity is worth more than most of the ruins in this dictionary, because a building still serving a congregation is doing what a church is for. “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8) is a proper affection; “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10) prefers the humblest place in it; and “mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7) names what the parishioners asked to keep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines parish as the precinct and inhabitants belonging to and attending a church; holm as a river isle, a low flat tract of rich land on the banks of a river; and congregation as an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
webster_full: PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
HOLM, n. An islet, or river isle; also, a low flat tract of rich land on the banks of a river.
CONGREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balustrade or railing of the choir to the chief entrance.
DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.
scriptures: Psa 26:8
LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Isa 56:7

Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: A Solway border abbey of 1150 whose nave the parishioners petitioned to keep: still their parish church, which is more than most of these houses can say.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain usefulness of a congregation's own building to the people who gather in it. “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching” (Heb 10:25) is about the assembling rather than the architecture, and a roof that keeps it dry is a mercy and not an idol.

The live corruption, which Christ named in the temple itself, is a house of prayer put to other uses: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Mat 21:13). Holm Cultram escaped the two opposite fates of these abbeys — the quarry and the country house — because ordinary people wanted it for what it was built for.
roots_summary: Old Norse holmr, a water-meadow; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Hebrew maon (H4583), a habitation; Greek ekklesia (G1577), an assembly; Greek episunagoge (G1997), a gathering together.
roots_lines: Old Norse holmr — an islet or water-meadow; the Norse layer in Cumberland place names.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house; “I have loved the habitation of thy house” (Psa 26:8).
Hebrew beth tephillah — house of prayer; “an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7).
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; the people, never the building.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — the assembling together; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).
usage: “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10) — the affection the parishioners acted on.
“make them joyful in my house of prayer” (Isa 56:7) — what the nave was kept for.
“but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Mat 21:13) — the fate it escaped.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Lincolnshire, founded 1143 as a daughter of Rievaulx, whose first abbot was Aelred)
etymology: Old Norse personal name with by, a farmstead or village: the settlement of a man named Refr. A Danelaw place name.
biblical_def: Revesby was founded in 1143 in the Lincolnshire fens by William de Roumare, a daughter of Rievaulx, and its first abbot was Aelred — who went on to rule Rievaulx itself and to write the Mirror of Charity and, most famously, De spiritali amicitia. Nothing of the abbey stands; the site is earthworks in a park. Its importance is its abbot's subject, because Aelred took friendship seriously as a Christian good at a time when much ascetic writing treated all affection as a distraction, and he was right to. Scripture is full of it. “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17); “there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother” (Pro 18:24); “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1Sa 18:1). And the Lord himself names his disciples by the word: “but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you” (Joh 15:15). Aelred's instinct was sound even where his framework was not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines friendship as an attachment to a person proceeding from intimate acquaintance and a reciprocation of kind offices; friend as one who is attached to another by affection; and charity as in a general sense love, benevolence, good will.
webster_full: FRIENDSHIP, n. An attachment to a person, proceeding from intimate acquaintance, and a reciprocation of kind offices, or from a favorable opinion of the amiable and respectable qualities of his mind.
FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company.
CHARITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; that disposition of heart which inclines men to think favorably of their fellow men, and to do them good.
AFFECTION, n. A bent of mind toward a particular object; also, in a more particular sense, a settled good will, love or zealous attachment.
INTIMATE, a. Inmost; inward; internal; also, near; close; as, intimate friendship.
scriptures: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
corruption_summary: A Lincolnshire daughter of Rievaulx whose first abbot was Aelred: a cloister that produced the age's best book on friendship, against an asceticism that distrusted affection.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is friendship as a Christian good and not a concession. “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up” (Ecc 4:10) is the plainest argument in Scripture against the solitary ideal, and Aelred, a monk, saw it.

The live corruption is the thinning of friendship into acquaintance and availability. Scripture's friend is a man who tells you the truth and stays — “Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel” (Pro 27:9) — and the measure is set impossibly high: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13).
roots_summary: Hebrew rea (H7453), a friend or companion; Hebrew ahab (H157), to love; Greek philos (G5384), a friend; Greek philia (G5373), friendship; Greek agapao (G25), to love.
roots_lines: Hebrew rea (H7453) — a friend, neighbour, companion; the word of the second great commandment.
Hebrew ahab (H157) — to love; “and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1Sa 18:1).
Greek philos (G5384) — a friend, one dear; “but I have called you friends” (Joh 15:15).
Greek philia (G5373) — friendship, affection; the word Aelred's treatise is built on.
Greek agapao (G25) — to love with settled goodwill; “Greater love hath no man than this” (Joh 15:13).
usage: “and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17) — friendship tested by trouble.
“woe to him that is alone when he falleth” (Ecc 4:10) — the case against solitude.
“all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you” (Joh 15:15) — friendship defined by disclosure.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Lincolnshire, founded 1139 in the Fountains line; one pier of its church stands, with its gate chapel intact nearby)
etymology: Old Norse kirkja, a church, with Old English stede, a place: the church place. A Danelaw name.
biblical_def: Kirkstead was founded in 1139 beside the Witham in Lincolnshire and became a substantial house in the Fountains filiation. What survives is a single tall fragment of the south transept standing alone in a field, and — a hundred yards off and perfectly intact — the thirteenth-century chapel of St Leonard at the gate, built for the lay people who were not admitted to the monks' church. The contrast is the entry. One building fell and the other stands, and the one that stands is the one the ordinary people used. The theology of the gate chapel is the problem: a church with an inner part for the religious and an outer provision for everybody else reproduces precisely the arrangement Christ abolished. “For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14); “Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus” (Heb 10:19); and “Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22). There is no gate chapel in the New Testament.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chapel as a house of worship, a place of worship subordinate to a church; partition as that by which separate parts are divided, a wall or division; and access as a coming to, near approach, admittance.
webster_full: CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship, subordinate to a parish church, or annexed to a palace or castle.
PARTITION, n. That by which separate parts are divided; a wall or other division between apartments.
ACCESS, n. A coming to; near approach; admittance; admission; as, to gain access to a prince.
HOLIEST, n. The most holy place; the inner sanctuary of the Jewish temple, entered only by the high priest.
VEIL, n. A cover; a curtain; something to intercept the view and hide an object; also, the curtain of the temple.
scriptures: Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh;
corruption_summary: A Lincolnshire house of 1139 reduced to one pier, with its gate chapel for lay people standing intact: a partition Christ had already broken down, rebuilt in stone.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the two-tier sanctuary, and it is the architectural form of the doctrine treated under evangelical counsels and third order. A monks' choir with a separate chapel for the laity at the gate says in stone what the system said in theology: that there are degrees of nearness to God. Scripture says the veil is torn — “By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” (Heb 10:20) — and every believer walks through it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is boldness. “boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus” (Heb 10:19) is addressed to brethren generally, not to a professed class, and “For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father” (Eph 2:18) makes the access one and the same for all.
roots_summary: Old Norse kirkja, a church; Greek mesotoichon (G3320), a middle wall; Greek parrhesia (G3954), boldness; Greek katapetasma (G2665), a veil; Greek prosagoge (G4318), access.
roots_lines: Old Norse kirkja with Old English stede — the church place; a Danelaw compound.
Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall; “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14).
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; “boldness to enter into the holiest” (Heb 10:19).
Greek katapetasma (G2665) — the temple veil; “through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” (Heb 10:20).
Greek prosagoge (G4318) — access, introduction; one access for all believers.
usage: “who hath made both one” (Eph 2:14) — the partition already gone when the chapel was built.
“Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22) — said to everybody.
“By a new and living way” (Heb 10:20) — the only entrance, and it is open.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Nottinghamshire, founded 1146 as a daughter of Rievaulx; its ranges became a great country house)
etymology: Old English ruh, rough, and ford: the rough ford. A Sherwood place name.
biblical_def: Rufford was founded in 1146 on the edge of Sherwood, a daughter of Rievaulx, and was never large. At the dissolution it was granted to the Earl of Shrewsbury, whose family turned the west range into a country house; the Savile family enlarged it, and Rufford Abbey spent four centuries as a gentleman's seat before passing to the county council as a park. Its history is the commonest English fate of these houses, and it is the one that should make a Protestant least comfortable, because the dissolution was not chiefly a reformation of doctrine at Rufford — it was a transfer of land to men who wanted it. Scripture has a settled view of that kind of transaction, and it does not soften for a godly pretext. “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!” (Isa 5:8); “And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage” (Mic 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines covet as to desire inordinately, to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess; dissolution as the act of dissolving, the breaking up of an assembly; and estate as property in land, or a fortune.
webster_full: COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess; in a bad sense.
DISSOLUTION, n. The act of dissolving or separating the parts; the breaking up of an assembly, or the putting an end to it.
ESTATE, n. Property in land or real estate; also, fortune; possessions; property in general.
GRANT, n. The act of granting or conveying; also, the thing granted or bestowed; a gift; a boon.
OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity, rigor or hardship.
scriptures: Isa 5:8
Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
Mic 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.

And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.
corruption_summary: A small Nottinghamshire house of 1146 granted at the dissolution and lived in as a country seat for four centuries: a transfer of land dressed as a reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name here is on the Protestant side of the ledger, and honesty requires naming it. Whatever was wrong in the monasteries — and this dictionary has said at length what was — the English dissolution enriched a class of courtiers, and the tenth commandment does not exempt them: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's” (Exo 20:17). Ahab had a legal mechanism too, and Elijah met him with “Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a true cause does not sanctify a greedy means. A reformation of the church's doctrine was necessary; the particular English method of effecting it put a great deal of land into particular hands, and “so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage” (Mic 2:2) is the prophet's word for that.
roots_summary: Old English ruh ford, the rough ford; Hebrew chamad (H2530), to covet; Hebrew gazal (H1497), to seize by violence; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness.
roots_lines: Old English ruh ford — the rough ford; a plain Sherwood topographic name.
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, covet; “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house” (Exo 20:17).
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, seize; “and take them by violence” (Mic 2:2).
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage; what Naboth would not sell.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the desire for more; Paul calls it idolatry.
usage: “that lay field to field, till there be no place” (Isa 5:8) — the woe on accumulation of estates.
“Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” (1Ki 21:19) — the prophet to a king with a legal title.
“nor any thing that is thy neighbour's” (Exo 20:17) — the commandment that exempts no cause.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Lincolnshire, founded 1147 in the Fountains line; the valley of God, quarried for Grimsthorpe Castle)
etymology: Latin vallis Dei, the valley of God, through Anglo-French vaudey; the same name as several continental houses.
biblical_def: Vaudey was founded in 1147 in south Lincolnshire, in the Fountains filiation, and bore the name vallis Dei, the valley of God. At the dissolution the site was granted to the Duke of Suffolk, and the abbey was taken down and its stone carted to build and enlarge Grimsthorpe Castle nearby. Nothing of the church is left above ground. A house named the valley of God dismantled to make a nobleman's house is the dissolution in a single image, and the prophet who speaks to it is Haggai, who found the people of Judah in the mirror position — their own houses finished, God's house a ruin: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). Christ's word over the temple covers the masonry: “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2). And the standing qualification over every building project is “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quarry as a place where stones are dug from the earth; castle as a house fortified for defense against an enemy, a fortress; and cieled, in the sense Haggai uses, as having the inner roof and walls overlaid with plaster or wainscot.
webster_full: QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
CASTLE, n. A house fortified for defense against an enemy; a fortress; the mansion of a nobleman.
CEIL, v.t. To overlay or cover the inner roof of a building; to cover the top or roof of a room.
DEMOLISH, v.t. To throw or pull down; to raze; to destroy, as a heap or structure; to ruin.
MATERIAL, n. The substance or matter of which any thing is made; as, the materials of a building.
scriptures: Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Mat 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Hag 1:9

Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the LORD of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house.
corruption_summary: A Lincolnshire house named the valley of God, pulled down at the dissolution and carted away to build a castle: Haggai's complaint exactly reversed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is Haggai's, and he states both halves of it. “Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the LORD of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house” (Hag 1:9) is addressed to men building their own houses out of God's. Grimsthorpe Castle is a handsome building made of a church, and the prophet has a word for the arrangement.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Psalm 127 opens with: “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1). Neither the abbey that was taken down nor the castle that was built up had any guarantee from God by virtue of being built, and a Christian who assumes his own projects do should read the psalm again.
roots_summary: Latin vallis Dei, valley of God; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Hebrew chareb (H2720), waste or desolate; Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone.
roots_lines: Latin vallis Dei — the valley of God; a name borne by several houses, and a large claim.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house; “Because of mine house that is waste” (Hag 1:9).
Hebrew chareb (H2720) — waste, desolate, dried up; Haggai's word for the unbuilt temple.
Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; the unit of both abbey and castle.
Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “There shall not be left here one stone upon another” (Mat 24:2).
usage: “and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4) — the prophet's question, reversed at Vaudey.
“ye run every man unto his own house” (Hag 1:9) — the diagnosis of a quarried abbey.
“Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1) — the condition over every building.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Leicestershire, founded 1133 as a daughter of Waverley; nothing of it remains above ground)
etymology: Old English, probably gara, a triangular strip of land, with dun, a hill: the hill by the gore of land.
biblical_def: Garendon was founded in 1133 in Leicestershire by the Earl of Leicester, a daughter of Waverley, and became the mother of Bordesley and Biddlesden and the grandmother of Stoneleigh. It therefore mattered: a modest house that planted others, which is the ordinary way institutions spread. Of the abbey itself there is nothing. The site passed to the Phillipps family, who built a hall and landscaped the park over it; the hall itself has since been demolished. Excavation has found footings and little else. An entity with descendants and no remains is a good occasion for the Psalmist's observation about the vanishing of what seemed solid: “Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found” (Psa 37:36), and Job's harder version: “The eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him” (Job 20:9). Both are said of men rather than monasteries, and that is the point — what Scripture says of a man's brief tenure is no less true of a corporation's long one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vanish as to disappear, to pass from a visible to an invisible state; remains as a dead body, and also that which is left; and oblivion as forgetfulness, cessation of remembrance.
webster_full: VANISH, v.i. To disappear; to pass from a visible to an invisible state; as, vapor vanishes from the sight.
REMAINS, n. That which is left; also, a dead body; and the works of an author after his decease.
OBLIVION, n. Forgetfulness; cessation of remembrance; also, a state of being forgotten.
FOOTING, n. Ground for the foot; support; basis; foundation; also, the lowest course of a wall.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
scriptures: Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found.
Job 20:9
The eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him.
For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more.
Ecc 1:11
There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after.
corruption_summary: A Leicestershire house of 1133 that planted Bordesley, Biddlesden and Stoneleigh and left no stone above ground: descendants and no remains.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the thorough realism of Scripture about being forgotten. “There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after” (Ecc 1:11) is not cynicism; it is the premise of a life lived for God rather than for a legacy.

The live corruption is the modern hunger for legacy — the ministry, platform or institution built so that a man's name continues. “For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more” (Psa 103:16) dismantles that project, and gently: what remains of Garendon is three abbeys' worth of descendants it never knew about, which is more than its founder was aiming at.
roots_summary: Hebrew zikkaron (H2146), a memorial; Hebrew maqom (H4725), a place; Hebrew abad (H6), to perish; Greek mnemosunon (G3422), a memorial; Hebrew hebel (H1892), vapour or vanity.
roots_lines: Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial, something that keeps remembrance.
Hebrew maqom (H4725) — a place; “neither shall his place any more behold him” (Job 20:9).
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, breath, vanity; the keyword of Ecclesiastes.
Hebrew abad (H6) — to perish, be lost; the fate of what is not kept by God.
Greek mnemosunon (G3422) — a memorial; what Christ promised the woman with the ointment, and he kept it.
usage: “I sought him, but he could not be found” (Psa 37:36) — the vanishing of what looked permanent.
“and the place thereof shall know it no more” (Psa 103:16) — said of a man, true of a house.
“There is no remembrance of former things” (Ecc 1:11) — the premise of living for God instead.

pos: n. (a small Cistercian abbey in Buckinghamshire, founded 1147 as a daughter of Garendon)
etymology: Old English personal name with denu, a valley: the valley of a man named Byttel. A Buckinghamshire name.
biblical_def: Biddlesden was founded in 1147 on the Buckinghamshire border, a daughter of Garendon, and was never anything but small and poor — a dozen or so monks, modest lands, and at the dissolution an income too slight to attract much notice. Its church site is occupied by an eighteenth-century house. It is in this dictionary precisely because it was unremarkable, since the great majority of religious houses were: the famous abbeys are a handful, and the ordinary one was a small community getting by on thin land. Scripture is deliberately generous to the small. “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10) is a rebuke to the man counting; “And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing” (Mar 12:42) is followed by Christ's verdict that she gave more than the rich; and “For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12) is the principle in a sentence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines small as slender, thin, fine, and of little moment or importance; mite as a very small particle or quantity, and a small piece of money; and poverty as destitution of property, indigence.
webster_full: SMALL, a. Slender; thin; fine; of little diameter; hence, of little size; not great; also, of little moment, importance or weight.
MITE, n. A very small particle or quantity; also, a small piece of money, said to be about one third of a farthing.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
OBSCURE, a. Dark; destitute of light; also, not easily understood; hidden; remote from observation; humble.
ACCEPT, v.t. To receive with a consenting mind; to receive with approbation or favor.
scriptures: Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing.
For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: A small poor Buckinghamshire house of 1147: unremarkable, which is what nearly every religious house actually was, and a thing Scripture is deliberately generous about.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's declared preference for what the world overlooks. “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27) is a statement of method, not a consolation prize.

The live corruption is the metric. Churches and ministries are assessed now by attendance, budget and reach, exactly as abbeys were assessed by income in 1535, and in both cases the small ones disappear from the account. “for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel” (Zec 4:10) puts the measuring line in God's hand rather than the auditor's.
roots_summary: Hebrew qaton (H6996), small; Hebrew meat (H4592), a little; Greek lepton (G3016), a mite; Greek asthenes (G772), weak; Greek euprosdektos (G2144), acceptable.
roots_lines: Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, young, insignificant; “the day of small things” (Zec 4:10).
Hebrew meat (H4592) — a little, a few; often what God works with.
Greek lepton (G3016) — a thin coin, a mite; “she threw in two mites, which make a farthing” (Mar 12:42).
Greek asthenes (G772) — weak, feeble; “God hath chosen the weak things of the world” (1Co 1:27).
Greek euprosdektos (G2144) — well accepted; what a willing mind makes a small gift.
usage: “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10) — a question put to the one keeping score.
“it is accepted according to that a man hath” (2Co 8:12) — the measure of a poor house's offering.
“to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27) — God's stated method.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Warwickshire, founded 1148 as a daughter of Bordesley; its gate chapel survives as the parish church)
etymology: Old English mere, a pool or lake, with vale, a valley: the valley of the pool.
biblical_def: Merevale was founded in 1148 in north Warwickshire, a daughter of Bordesley, and little of the abbey proper survives beyond fragments and earthworks. Its gate chapel does survive, entire, and has been the parish church of Merevale since the dissolution — the same arrangement as at Kirkstead, with the opposite outcome, since here the lay chapel was not merely left standing but taken over as the congregation's own. Having stated the objection to gate chapels under Kirkstead, this entry states the better half of the story: the building put up to keep the laity at the gate became the building in which the laity are the church. That is the Reformation in one parish, and Scripture supplies the warrant for the whole direction of travel: “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9). A people called a priesthood needs no outer court.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chapel as a place of worship subordinate to a parish church; parish as the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church; and priesthood as the office or character of a priest, and the order of men set apart for sacred offices.
webster_full: CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship subordinate to a parish church, or annexed to a mansion or castle.
PARISH, n. The precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church; also, the inhabitants themselves.
PRIESTHOOD, n. The office or character of a priest; also, the order of men set apart for sacred offices.
MERE, n. A pool or lake; a standing water; also, a boundary.
VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Rev 1:6
And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
Eph 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
corruption_summary: A Warwickshire house of 1148 whose gate chapel for the laity became, and remains, the parish church: a building raised to keep people out, now the church they are.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the priesthood of all believers, which is not a slogan but a text: “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen” (Rev 1:6). Everything the gate chapel implied about degrees of access is answered by it.

The live corruption is the quiet return of a clerical caste in Protestant dress: the professional who prays, studies and administers while the congregation watches. “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices” (1Pe 2:5) gives the whole body the offering to make, and “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Eph 2:19) settles the standing of everyone in the room.
roots_summary: Greek hierateuma (G2406), a priesthood; Greek laos (G2992), a people; Greek sumpolites (G4847), a fellowcitizen; Greek oikeios (G3609), of the household; Hebrew mamlakah (H4467), a kingdom.
roots_lines: Greek hierateuma (G2406) — a priesthood; “a royal priesthood, an holy nation” (1Pe 2:9).
Greek laos (G2992) — a people; the root of laity, and a word of honour.
Greek sumpolites (G4847) — a fellowcitizen; “but fellowcitizens with the saints” (Eph 2:19).
Greek oikeios (G3609) — belonging to a household; the status of every believer.
Greek basileia (G932) — a kingdom; “And hath made us kings and priests unto God” (Rev 1:6).
usage: “that ye should shew forth the praises of him” (1Pe 2:9) — the whole people given the work of praise.
“hath made us kings and priests unto God” (Rev 1:6) — the end of an outer court.
“ye are no more strangers and foreigners” (Eph 2:19) — the standing of the people at the gate.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Worcestershire, founded 1138 as a daughter of Garendon; mother of Merevale and Stoneleigh)
etymology: Old English personal or descriptive element with leah, a clearing or meadow; the clearing by the border or boards.
biblical_def: Bordesley was founded in 1138 in the Arrow valley of Worcestershire, a daughter of Garendon, and became in turn the mother of Merevale and Stoneleigh. It was a working abbey of the ordinary English kind, with mills and iron-working on the site, and it has been extensively excavated — the published digs at Bordesley are among the main sources for what a Cistercian industrial complex actually looked like. What survives is therefore knowledge rather than architecture. As a mother house it illustrates the expansive instinct of the order, and Scripture's own image for expansion is a tent rather than a castle: “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2). The command is to enlarge and to strengthen in the same breath, which is the thing institutions find hardest; the Cistercian expansion was spectacular and its stakes were not strengthened at the same rate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines enlarge as to make greater in quantity or dimensions, to extend in limits; stake as a small piece of wood sharpened and set in the ground, as for a fence or a tent; and increase as augmentation, growth, extension.
webster_full: ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size; to expand or extend.
STAKE, n. A small piece of wood or timber, sharpened at one end and set in the ground, or prepared for setting, as for a fence or a tent.
INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; extension; also, that which is added; profit; interest.
CORD, n. A string, or small rope, composed of several strands twisted together.
FORGE, n. A furnace in which iron or other metal is heated and hammered into form; also, the place where such work is done.
scriptures: Isa 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
Isa 54:3
For thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles, and make the desolate cities to be inhabited.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.
corruption_summary: A working Worcestershire abbey of 1138 with mills and ironworks, mother of Merevale and Stoneleigh: enlargement without a matching strengthening of stakes.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is growth outrunning foundation, and Christ states it as a parable about building: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luk 14:28), with the outcome in the next breath — “This man began to build, and was not able to finish” (Luk 14:30). The Cistercian order planted some seven hundred houses in a century and a half and could not sustain the discipline of them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's pairing: “For thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles, and make the desolate cities to be inhabited” (Isa 54:3) promises real expansion, but the preceding verse requires lengthened cords and strengthened stakes, and a movement that does only the first will tear.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachab (H7337), to be wide or enlarge; Hebrew yathed (H3489), a tent peg; Hebrew chezeq from chazaq (H2388), to strengthen; Greek oikodomeo (G3618), to build; Greek dapane (G1160), cost.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachab (H7337) — to be broad, to enlarge; “Enlarge the place of thy tent” (Isa 54:2).
Hebrew yathed (H3489) — a tent peg or stake; “and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2).
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen; the verb Isaiah pairs with enlarging.
Greek oikodomeo (G3618) — to build; the verb of Christ's parable about a tower.
Greek dapane (G1160) — cost, expense; “and counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28).
usage: “spare not, lengthen thy cords” (Isa 54:2) — the command to expand.
“and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2) — the clause expansion forgets.
“This man began to build, and was not able to finish” (Luk 14:30) — the result of omitting it.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Warwickshire, founded 1154 as a daughter of Bordesley; now Stoneleigh Abbey, a great country house)
etymology: Old English stan, stone, and leah, a clearing or meadow: the stony clearing, on the Avon.
biblical_def: Stoneleigh was founded in 1154 beside the Avon in Warwickshire, a daughter of Bordesley, after earlier attempts at other sites. At the dissolution it passed by purchase to the Leigh family, who kept it for four centuries and built, around and over the monastic remains, one of the grandest baroque houses in England; Jane Austen's mother was a Leigh, and Austen visited. The gatehouse and part of the abbey survive inside the mansion. The house is magnificent and the question it raises is Solomon's, who built on a scale nobody since has matched and then wrote the audit. “I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards” (Ecc 2:4) runs through several verses of accumulation to a conclusion that has never been improved on: “Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun” (Ecc 2:11). A monastery that became a mansion has had both halves of Ecclesiastes 2 performed on its own ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mansion as a house, a dwelling place of considerable size and dignity; magnificence as grandeur of appearance, splendor of show or state; and vanity as emptiness, want of substance to satisfy desire, fruitless desire or endeavor.
webster_full: MANSION, n. Any place of residence; a house; a habitation; particularly, a dwelling place of some size and dignity.
MAGNIFICENCE, n. Grandeur of appearance; greatness and splendor of show or state.
VANITY, n. Emptiness; want of substance to satisfy desire; uncertainty; inanity; also, fruitless desire or endeavor.
VEXATION, n. The act of irritating, or making uneasy; disquiet; agitation; uneasiness; trouble.
PROFIT, n. Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labor or exertion.
scriptures: Ecc 2:4
I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards:
Ecc 2:11
Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
corruption_summary: A Warwickshire house of 1154 that became one of the grandest baroque mansions in England: both halves of Ecclesiastes 2 performed on one piece of ground.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is Solomon's own and he published it. A man builds great works and then looks at them: “and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun” (Ecc 2:11). Christ makes the same point with a shorter timescale and a harder ending: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Luk 12:20).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the only investment Scripture calls secure: “But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal” (Mat 6:20). Neither the abbey nor the mansion was that, and the gatehouse standing inside the great house is a reasonably eloquent way of saying so.
roots_summary: Old English stan leah, stony clearing; Hebrew hebel (H1892), vanity or vapour; Hebrew yithron (H3504), profit; Greek thesauros (G2344), treasure; Greek aphron (G878), a fool.
roots_lines: Old English stan leah — the stony clearing; a plain Warwickshire name.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, breath, vanity; “all was vanity and vexation of spirit” (Ecc 2:11).
Hebrew yithron (H3504) — profit, advantage, what is left over; the thing Solomon looked for and did not find.
Greek thesauros (G2344) — a treasure, storehouse; “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:20).
Greek aphron (G878) — senseless, a fool; “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” (Luk 12:20).
usage: “I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards” (Ecc 2:4) — the project, stated by its builder.
“there was no profit under the sun” (Ecc 2:11) — the audit, by the same hand.
“where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20) — the one secure holding.
